nameStory: This plant gets its name from two sources: its arrow-shaped seed pods that point skyward like tiny green arrows, and the Gaspé Peninsula in Quebec where it was first scientifically described. The 'arrowgrass' part comes from its grass-like leaves and those distinctive pointed fruits that early botanists thought resembled arrowheads.
description: Gaspé Peninsula Arrowgrass is a small, grass-like plant that grows in the salty tidal zones along New England's coast. It forms low clumps of narrow, fleshy leaves that emerge directly from the ground without a visible stem. The plant sends up slender spikes of tiny, inconspicuous greenish flowers that develop into the characteristic arrow-shaped seed pods. This hardy little plant rarely grows taller than 6-12 inches, making it easy to overlook among other salt marsh vegetation.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Three-pointed seed pods that look like tiny green arrows pointing upward, about the size of a grain of rice. They feel firm and slightly waxy to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves that feel thick and fleshy, almost succulent-like, with a slightly salty taste if nibbled. They grow in small clumps directly from the base.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny greenish flowers arranged on slender spikes that rise above the leaves. Individual flowers are so small they're barely noticeable without close inspection.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small, tight clumps or patches in the intertidal zone, often partially buried in sand or mud. Plants look like miniature grass tufts.

idTips.label: Habitat Location
idTips.description: Always found in areas that get covered by seawater at high tide, often with a briny smell and salt crystals visible on nearby surfaces when dry.

habitat: Look for this rare plant in the tidal zones of Maine's Atlantic coast, specifically in areas that flood during high tide. It grows in sandy or muddy salt marshes, often mixed with other salt-tolerant plants like glasswort and salt marsh asters. You'll need to time your search for low tide when these areas are accessible and not underwater.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as bright green tufts, and the plant begins its growing season as warmer weather arrives.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs during summer months, with tiny greenish flower spikes rising above the leaf clumps. This is the best time to spot the plant when it's most visible.
seasonality.fall: The distinctive arrow-shaped seed pods mature and become most prominent, making this the easiest season for positive identification.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back significantly or go dormant, making identification very difficult during the coldest months.

funFact: This plant is so rare in New England that it has been spotted only 13 times by naturalists, making it one of the most elusive native plants in the region - you're more likely to see a bald eagle than find one of these tiny coastal treasures!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other small grasses or sedges growing in salt marshes, but the distinctive three-pointed arrow seed pods are a dead giveaway. Remember: if it's in the tide zone and has tiny green arrows for seeds, you've found something very special.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting it's limited to the Gaspé Peninsula, this plant actually has a broader range along the Atlantic coast of eastern Canada and Maine. The name can be misleading since the Gaspé Peninsula is just where scientists first formally described it in 1961.
compareHints: Gaspé Peninsula Arrowgrass is much smaller and rarer than its relative, common arrowgrass, which grows taller and is more widespread. The common arrowgrass typically has six-pointed seed pods rather than the three-pointed pods of the Gaspé species, and it often grows in less salty conditions like freshwater marshes. If you find arrowgrass in a purely saltwater tidal zone with three-pointed pods, you've likely found the rare Gaspé variety.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common arrowgrass is much more widespread than its rare relative, Gaspé Peninsula arrowgrass, which is found only in a few locations in northern New England.
